IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Editorial: “Unkind cuts” — ECI’s voter deletions

Core Idea

Editorial questions the large-scale deletion of voters during the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka.

1. Scale of deletions

Around 22% voters in Telangana and 19.5% in Karnataka were reportedly deleted.

Bengaluru saw some constituencies losing more than half their electors.

Hyderabad had several constituencies with over 40% deletions.

Such massive deletions cannot simply be dismissed as routine cleaning of electoral rolls.

2. Why is it problematic?

If voters have merely migrated within the same State, their names should be shifted rather than deleted.

The editorial argues that available survey and population data do not sufficiently justify such large reductions.

Therefore, transparency + verification become essential.

3. Democratic concern

The right to vote is central to universal adult franchise.
Wrongful deletion can lead to disenfranchisement—a citizen being effectively excluded from democratic participation.

4. Institutional accountability

ECI has reportedly not provided adequate elector-to-population ratios and detailed deletion data.

Karnataka’s deletion lists lacked easily verifiable details such as old booth numbers, making verification difficult.

Political parties and citizens also need to actively file objections.

5. Larger lesson

Electoral-roll revision is necessary to remove dead, duplicate or shifted voters, but the process must never sacrifice legitimate voters.

Way Forward:
Transparency → searchable deletion lists → door-to-door verification → easy claims & objections → independent audit → timely restoration of wrongly deleted names.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

The programme was framed under #ChinaMustAnswer.

Its disaster footage was catalogued and repeatedly displayed while claims were made concerning “deep cutting” into the mountain shelf, ecological disturbance and a “near seismic event.”

Then came the challenge connecting the alleged threat in Pakistan with the people dying in Nepal.

That creates a causal insinuation of extraordinary seriousness.

So answer the elementary questions:

Which dam? Which tunnel? Which excavation? Which release? Which operating instruction? Which geological finding?

What evidence did Republic possess, at the time of transmission, establishing that Chinese activity caused or materially contributed to this particular catastrophe?

The Himalaya can produce catastrophic rock-and-ice failures without hostile human intervention. India knows this from its own territory. The February 2021 Chamoli disaster in Uttarakhand involved an enormous rock-and-ice avalanche that transformed into a devastating debris flow, destroyed hydropower infrastructure and killed more than two hundred people.

Chamoli does not prove what happened in Nepal.

That is exactly the point.

One Himalayan catastrophe cannot prove the cause of another.

Causation requires evidence.

If Republic had that evidence, publish it.

If Republic did not have it, explain why culpability was suggested while the dead were still being counted.

IV. “THE ANSWER IS NO.” NO TO WHAT?

Then Republic turned to the Indus.

The programme asked:

“Have we done any diversion works or any building even after we suspended the Indus Waters Treaty?”

It asked whether India had undertaken any infrastructural change.

And then came the categorical answer:

“The answer is no.”

No?

In the same programme, your presenter raised a newspaper clipping before the camera carrying the headline:

“Our share of river waters will no more go to Pakistan: PM Modi.”

The wider public record is equally impossible to compress into the word “no.”

India has announced that it considers the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance. Indian ministers have publicly spoken about preventing water from reaching Pakistan. Reuters reported in May 2025, citing government documents and people familiar with the planning, that projects affecting the western rivers were being accelerated.

The Ranbir Canal has been discussed.

Kiru exists.

There is nothing inherently improper about India constructing infrastructure consistent with its legal position. That is not my allegation.

My challenge is to the categorical statement:

“The answer is no.”

No infrastructure?

No new works?

No diversion?

No planning?

No operational change?

No project capable of altering timing or control?

Or merely no work Republic considers prohibited under India’s interpretation of the Treaty?

Those are radically different propositions.

Which one did you mean?

And there is a larger contradiction.

You condemn cutting into the Himalaya when discussing China.

Then look with the same seriousness at the Chenab and Jhelum systems and at Indian Himalayan engineering generally: dams, tunnels, hydropower projects, access works, barrages and proposed diversions.

If cutting into this mountain system is environmentally relevant when China does it, it remains environmentally relevant when India does it.

Scrutinise both.
3/6

I make no allegation that aggressive or inaccurate journalism is, by itself, an international crime. I do not accuse Republic of a crime against humanity. I will not misuse legal language merely because it sounds powerful.

Article 20(2) of the ICCPR addresses the narrower subject of advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred constituting incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence. The Rabat Plan of Action identifies factors including context, speaker, intent, content and form, extent of dissemination and likelihood of harm.

I do not pronounce that threshold crossed here.

I ask something more elementary:

What evidence justified telling a mass audience that a named foreign public figure had threatened Indians with death by water and then connecting that alleged threat to people dying in Nepal?

J’ACCUSE

Mr Goswami, you spent the programme demanding that China answer.

Now answer for Republic.

You said Victor Gao threatened India with water.

Produce the threat.

You invoked killing Indians with water.

Produce the complete sentence and context.

You connected those allegations with Nepal.

Produce the causal evidence.

You said India had undertaken no diversion works, building or infrastructural change.

Explain “the answer is no” against the documentary record.

You condemn cutting and engineering in the Himalaya when discussing China.

Then examine Indian Himalayan cutting, tunnelling, barrages and hydropower construction by the same standard.

You accuse another man of weaponising water.

Define weaponisation and apply your definition irrespective of nationality.

You demand accountability from the country upstream of India.

Accept the legitimacy of downstream accountability as well.

You characterised a statement of reciprocity as a threat.

Show us the words that threaten.

This is my challenge:

Defy the evidence.

Not with another monologue.

Not with another hashtag.

Not with nationality.

With documents.

With recordings.

With dates.

With engineering records.

With the complete Gao quotation.

With the geological evidence.

With the public record.

Much of the material I rely upon comes not from China and not from Pakistan but from Indian public statements, Indian reporting, publicly documented projects, international reporting based on Indian government material, and Republic’s own broadcast.

Read my case.

Read IL-1 to IL-15.

Then answer it.

FORMAL REQUEST FOR SUBSTANTIATION, CORRECTION AND RETRACTION

I request that Republic preserve the complete broadcast and underlying editorial material relevant to the allegations examined here, including the source upon which statements attributed to Victor Gao were based.

I request publication of the complete source and context for the allegation that Mr Gao advocated weaponising rivers against India or killing Indians with water.

I request publication of the evidentiary basis existing at transmission for associating Chinese conduct with the Nepal catastrophe.

I request clarification of what Republic meant by the categorical assertion “the answer is no” concerning Indian diversion works, building or infrastructural change.

Where Republic can substantiate its factual propositions:

Publish the evidence.

Where Republic demonstrates that my account is materially wrong:

Tell me precisely where and produce the evidence. I will correct it publicly.

But where Republic cannot substantiate a serious factual allegation it broadcast and subsequently republished, I request that Republic correct and, where appropriate, retract that allegation with prominence reasonably commensurate with that given to the original publication.

I seek no censorship.

I seek no ban.

I seek no government suppression of Republic.

I seek accountability through evidence.

VICTOR GAO WILL DECIDE FOR VICTOR GAO. I HAVE DECIDED FOR MYSELF.

Mr Goswami raised the possibility on air that Victor Gao might sue him.

That remark is, in a sense, why this document exists.
4/6

India’s global image is facing a sharp decline, with new polling showing rising unfavourable views across the United States and other democracies. Critics have linked the backlash to concerns over minority rights, internet shutdowns, press freedom and crackdowns on dissent under the Modi era. 

#NarendraModi #India #HumanRights #PressFreedom

As an Indian did you celebrate Meta making Kunal Shah the boss of WhatsApp? And then immediately you thought how a foreign company is about to run the rails of 1.5 billion people?

China saw this coming and built WeChat (social feed, messaging, and payments fused into one platform, wired into how the state governs). But China's model is the CCP's model. One party, top-down control, surveillance as the default, dissent erased. That works for an authoritarian state. It's the opposite of what India is.

India is a liberal democracy. Many parties, free press that can taunt Modi’s 56 inches, and 1.5 billion people who are allowed to disagree out loud. So India can't just copy WeChat. As an Indian founder, can you build a platform that gives the state the tools to keep the peace in the world's most diverse country, without handing it a CCP-style kill switch? I think you can. I prototyped what it could look like.

You start with one truth: governing a country as diverse as India is, fundamentally, an exercise in managing information. One wrong post in the wrong town at the wrong hour becomes a riot. X and WhatsApp are built to resist the government intervention as they are US based companies. US is unique in the world when it comes to freedom of expression. So by default, X/WhatsApp don't bend for the local context. A platform tuned to India would do the opposite, without becoming a censorship machine. Here's how:

1. Graduated, time-bound information control with in-built accountability
The local administrator (the DM) can block a single post for up to 24 hours. Just long enough to defuse an emerging riot-like situation on the ground, immediately, while tempers cool. If they need longer, the system forces them to seek a one-week extension from the State's Chief Minister. And a permanent takedown can't be done locally at all. That request is channeled up to the Home Minister or CIC. This ensures that no one person can quietly bury something forever. Every level of control has a higher level watching it. This is the line between India and China. Not CCP “censorship but but control that is checked at every step.
2. Political hierarchy that mirrors India's actual structure.
Unlike China's one party, India has many. Some of these are regional and faith based. Irrespective of ideology, parties can build their real hierarchy inside the platform: national → state → district → block → village. The booth-level worker in a village and the national leadership are part of one verifiable chain, instead of a chaos of anonymous handles claiming to speak for a party. The structure is in built to transfer mantle of local MP to another person belong to a different party as new election results get declared. With Uttar Pradesh being the most politically active state, I think the app should start from UP. BJP, SP, and Congress provide enough fuel for rapid adoption.
3. Trust-based verification without intrusive government ID that fights bots.
Many LefT leaning Indians shame India for being a low-trust society. The reality is quite different. India is very high trust. The platform leverages this high trust for verification. Verification starts with officials and party representatives as the root authorities. But from there, anyone who is verified can verify people they personally know. No demand for a driving licence or Aadhaar to exist on the platform. No central database of who you are. The genius is in the accountability. Every verification leaves a trail. The moment a fake account is caught, the system analyzes who verified them and re-examines everyone that account went on to verify. Fraud, once detected, unravels the whole branch. That makes fake networks expensive to build and easy to squash.
4. Festivals, localized to your district where anyone can become a local celebrity.
India is a land of festivals, and festivals are deeply local. What one district celebrates isn't what the next one does. So every user picks their district, and the app's world is shaped around it. Folks in Saharanpur see their background change to Shakumbhari Devi in season, while folks in Meerut see Nauchandi. If you are a Muslim, your wallpaper says Eid Mubarak during Eid. Users still have a say in what they see, but the default is home. This turns festivals into community engines. On Diwali, people across a district post their rangoli, and neighbors from the same district upvote the ones they love. An ordinary person can become a local celebrity overnight, recognized by the people who actually live around them. A local batting star from Balia can catch eyes of state cricket team selectors after smashing 6-sixes in an over. And a state can lift this up a level, running the same celebration as a state-wide competition that builds community across districts. Festivals stop being a feed of strangers and become your town, at its best.
 5. Private messaging with the network you already trust. The same web of verified relationships that powers your feed also powers your inbox. Message your Nani two districts away or the school friend living next door, all within a network where the person on the other end is who they say they are. Because messaging rides on the same trust graph as verification, it inherits the same protection. The bot farms and unknown numbers that flood WhatsApp don't get a way in. Your conversations stay among the people who are actually part of your world, from family scattered across the state to the neighbor you've known since elementary school.

This is a WeChat designed for India's rich diversity and unique challenges. Fast where it needs to be, accountable where it must be, built on trust instead of surveillance, and rooted in the place you actually call home. Neither China's kill switch nor Silicon Valley's 3rd world arrogance. India's own.

A Student Spoke About an Unpaid Scholarship. The Journalist Reported It. Then Came the FIRs.

[Newslaundry — Khushi Mehrotra’s report]
https://t.co/4kxMks4eKh

What began as a student's complaint about an unpaid scholarship at COEP Technological University, Pune, has escalated into a political and legal battle involving rival student organisations, a campus confrontation and three FIRs—including one naming the journalist who reported the student's grievance. 

ABP Majha journalist Mandar Gonjari interviewed students at COEP ahead of Rahul Gandhi's Chhatron Ki Goonj programme. Among them was Sampada Pramod Bade, who said she had not received her scholarship for three years and had allegedly been charged fees under the general category despite being admitted under the orphan quota. Other students reportedly raised scholarship and hostel-related concerns as well. 

The report subsequently became politically useful to both sides. Congress's media cell circulated part of the report to challenge Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis's claim that students attending Gandhi's programme were from Congress-run institutions. 

Then the student's account changed.

Gonjari alleges that ABVP activists pressured Bade to retract her earlier statements, saying that the journalist had manipulated her and that her scholarship grievance was not genuine. Bade subsequently released a video saying that pressure had been created and that she had been manipulated. BJP also circulated another video in which she appealed for her campus to be freed from political activity. ABVP denies pressuring her. 

The dispute then escalated into an ABVP–NSUI confrontation on August 21.

Three FIRs followed:

An ABVP complaint alleged assault and pressure on the student by NSUI/Congress workers.

A Youth Congress complaint alleged that Bade was confined in the hostel and that Congress workers were assaulted.

A COEP administration complaint alleged trespassing by NSUI/Congress workers and also named journalist Mandar Gonjari over alleged unauthorised entry. 

There is an important distinction here: the FIR does not allege that Gonjari participated in the alleged violence or sloganeering. Gonjari denies entering the hostel and says the interviews were recorded in an open area near the college canteen, in daylight, with other journalists and security personnel present. The police say the matter is under investigation. 

The Pune Union of Working Journalists has condemned the journalist's inclusion and asked the police commissioner to remove him from the case. 

There is also an important unresolved question about the scholarship itself. A Youth Congress representative told Newslaundry that the scholarship money was released after the ABP Majha report went viral—but that claim comes from the political representative and should not be presented as independently established fact without further documentation. COEP itself confirms that it administers numerous government and other scholarships. 

The fundamental issue

A student raises a legitimate grievance.

A journalist investigates and reports it.

Political organisations then contest the narrative.

A campus confrontation follows.

And suddenly the journalist himself becomes a criminal accused.

That should concern everyone who believes in a free press.

Journalists must of course be accountable if they actually trespass, fabricate evidence or participate in violence. But those allegations must be established through evidence—not manufactured through political pressure.

The police must therefore investigate all sides impartially:

Was the student's original scholarship grievance genuine?
Why did her account subsequently change?
Was she pressured by anyone?
What does the CCTV footage show?
Where exactly was the journalist when he conducted the interview?
Did he enter the hostel at all?
Who initiated the campus violence?
And why ...Cont'd

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Over the last few weeks, two of my Instagram posts were withheld in India. One questioned RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s position on LGBTQ rights. The other shared Arundhati Roy’s observation about how Gen Z protests have challenged and dismantled the carefully cultivated political persona of Narendra Modi. (Screenshots of Meta’s notices are attached)

I have reason to believe that many political posts, mine included, have been shadow-banned & are reaching far fewer people than they recently did. Many have expressed similar concerns. At the same time, we are seeing repeated disruptions and adjournments whenever uncomfortable issues arise in Parliament.

Recent reports suggest that Sonia Gandhi’s memoir is no longer moving forward with Penguin India, following disagreements over aspects of the manuscript.
Among the reported points of contention are comparisons between Narendra Modi and previous Prime Ministers, and references to the India-China border situation.

What fascinates me is not the censorship itself, but the psychology behind it.

People often imagine that suppressing information makes it disappear. In reality, the opposite frequently happens.

Psychologists call it the “Streisand Effect”. Attempts to hide, censor or suppress information often increase public curiosity about it. The forbidden becomes irresistible. The hidden becomes desirable. The thing you tell people not to look at suddenly becomes the only thing they want to look at.

Human beings are wired that way.

Tell a child not to open a cupboard and that cupboard instantly becomes the most interesting object in the house.

Tell citizens not to read a book, and they start searching for PDFs.

Ban a film, and people who had no intention of watching it suddenly queue up to see what all the fuss is about.

I’ve understood this for years, which is why I have consistently opposed censorship, even when it involves work or people I disagree with.

I have argued against attempts to suppress films across the political spectrum. Whether it was Haider, Padmaavat, The Kerala Story or The Kashmir Files, my position has remained the same: if you disagree with a film, critique it, debate it, challenge it, boycott it if you wish. But don’t ban it.

The moment we start demanding that books, films, speeches and ideas be removed because they offend us, we hand the same weapon to those who wish to silence us.

I may find many things RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat says deeply problematic, but I would never support demands to cancel his rally, ban his speech or prevent him from addressing an audience. People have the right to hear him and make up their own minds.

Freedom of expression cannot be reserved only for views we approve of.

And this is why recent developments should concern everyone, regardless of political affiliation.

If publishers, platforms, institutions and governments become increasingly fearful of criticism, scrutiny or inconvenient questions, the damage extends far beyond a single book, a single post or a single political figure.

And finally, a warning to those big men with little courage. 

History has never been kind to those who tried to control thought. Not kings, not dictators, not religious authorities, not governments, not corporations, and certainly not politicians convinced of their own invincibility. They all eventually discover the truth that ideas are very difficult things to imprison.

Because every now and then, an idea that was ordered to die in a prison cell grows too large to be contained, breaks out, and returns as a movement, or even a revolution.

text:
A Delhi High Court order has once again had to remind the Grievance Appellate Committee to follow the timeline already prescribed under the IT Rules, 2021. On 20 August 2026, the Court directed the GAC to decide the appeal of content creator Riya, whose Instagram account #riaspeaks has over five lakh followers, within 30 days. Her appeal had already been pending for more than 42 days. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/26gA6SeMe0

The GAC is particularly important because it is supposed to provide users with an appellate remedy against intermediary decisions, including arbitrary or permanent account bans. Yet when an appeal itself remains pending beyond the prescribed period, a creator can be left with no meaningful remedy except approaching a High Court. The burden then falls on users and the judiciary alike. (6/7)

IFF had earlier suggested increasing the number of GACs to deal with the growing volume of appeals and making GAC orders publicly accessible, given the quasi-adjudicatory nature of their work. Neither has happened. We are assisting Riya through the appeal process and will continue to monitor the matter. (7/7)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX
